title: Bit-significance placement: exponent in strong rows, mantissa in leaky
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: the controller splits BF16/FP8 tensors so sign/exponent bits go to fully refreshed, ECC-protected rows while low mantissa bits go to rows refreshed 16x less often or to weak-binned dies, sold as an AI-grade memory SKU.
why: ~50% of AI-resident bits escape the refresh and tail spec: ~40% less refresh energy, and weak dies otherwise scrapped become sellable capacity.

title: Thin-film thermometer per mat drives local refresh rates
idea: Inverts 'one temperature sensor per die': the single added mask patterns a TaN thin-film resistor meandering over each mat, read by the periphery to scale each mat's refresh to its own temperature, since mats under hot compute dies differ by 10-20 C.
why: Most mats refresh at their cooler local rate; 30-50% refresh cut in HBM and 3D stacks with thermal gradients (facts 3, 6).

title: Shaped wordline falling edge and capped row-open time
idea: Ideal: activating a row disturbs nothing. Closest: the wordline driver uses a slow, shaped falling ramp (~5 ns) instead of a sharp edge to cut electron injection and capacitive kick into adjacent rows, and the controller closes rows after <=36 ns to avoid RowPress-style long-open disturbance.
why: Fact 9: may raise the effective hammer threshold 3-10x at small latency cost, reducing mitigation refreshes.

title: Heterochromatin silencing: ship dies with no repair, OS silences bad regions
idea: Cells silence unusable genome stretches as heterochromatin instead of repairing them; design ultra-cheap-process dies with zero spare rows/columns, no fuse banks and no repair test step, store a boot-time silence map, and let the OS never allocate silenced regions, selling each die by its actual capacity.
why: Repair test time and redundancy scale with defect density and would kill a ~100x-cheaper high-defect process; removing them (plus ~3-5% spare area and fuse periphery) keeps such processes economic.

title: Sub-critical stochastic MTJ writes with ECC absorbing misses
idea: Box [medium: perpendicular MTJ | access: spin-orbit-torque line | sense: TMR at 50 mV bias | integration: BEOL over CMOS | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Writes use a short pulse at ~60% of deterministic switching current so ~1e-3 of bits fail to switch; instead of write-verify loops, a BCH code over each 512-bit word absorbs them and background scrubbing rewrites only failed bits.
why: Constraint: write energy ~5-10x lower and low-bias reads keep read energy small; byte-addressable nonvolatile cell with no refresh.

title: Buy untested die by the kilogram, grade them in-system
idea: Inverts 'the vendor tests and bins every die': hyperscalers buy dies with only gross-function test, skipping hours of retention and speed test, at a discount; servers run a self-test boot phase, build each die's weak-cell map and place data by quality tier.
why: Test is ~10-15% of DRAM cost and binning discards marginal die; raises usable supply 5-10% and lowers cost per bit.

title: Capacity-elastic twin-cell mode for deep sleep
idea: Po: memory that doubles itself to fall asleep. When a device idles, the controller compacts live data into half the rows and rewrites each bit into two cells on complementary bitlines; twin-cell differential sensing doubles signal, so self-refresh stretches from 64 ms to ~1 s.
why: Idle power (fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle): self-refresh power down ~10x during idle periods, at a temporary 2x capacity cost.

title: 2050 engineer: every printed word carries its own reference pair
idea: A 2050 engineer assumes devices vary by 30% and designs around it: each 32-bit printed word includes a '1' and a '0' reference cell written in the same pulse, and on read the comparator uses the midpoint of those two local references, cancelling device-to-device Vth spread, drift since write and temperature to first order.
why: Printed TFT variation (sigma Vth ~0.2-0.5 V) defeats global references; local self-referencing cuts the required signal margin ~3x at 6% bit overhead.

title: Synonymous-codon encoding that hides known weak cells
idea: Synonymous codons let DNA tolerate mutations without changing the protein. Each 8-bit symbol is written into 9 cells. Using the row's known weak-cell map, and the fact that a true cell leaks only 1->0, the encoder picks the synonymous codeword that places a discharged '0' in every known leaky cell (Kuznetsov-Tsybakov coding for memory with defects). Weak cells then never hold charge that can leak.
why: With ~12% overhead, cells with poor retention (fact 3) stay in service and refresh is no longer set by the tail. Refresh could stretch 4-8x for rows with mapped defects.

title: Minify neighbor coupling with dynamic negative bias on adjacent wordlines
idea: While a row is open, drive its two neighbor wordlines further negative (about -0.3 to -0.6 V) for the open duration. This raises their access transistors' barrier against passing-gate and coupling-induced charge loss.
why: Fact 9: could raise the hammer threshold several-fold above ~1k activations, with changes only in the local wordline drivers.

title: Conductive ferroelectric domain-wall cell with non-destructive read
idea: Charged domain walls in LiNbO3/BiFeO3 films conduct 1e3-1e6x more than the bulk. Write by creating or erasing a wall segment between two electrodes with a sub-ns lateral field pulse. Read the wall current without switching polarization, unlike FeRAM's destructive read. The state is polarization topology, so no charge leaks.
why: Destructive read (fact 8) and refresh (fact 3) both removed. Wall pinning, the residual failure mode, is handled by write-verify plus ECC.

title: Na: rock-salt lattice data inversion picks least-hammerable neighbor pattern
idea: Like Na+ and Cl- alternating in a crystal, controller RTL XORs data with a physical-row-parity mask (learned from the DIMM's address scramble) chosen per module after profiling which neighbor charge relation (same or opposite) flips least, so adjacent rows mostly hold the benign pattern. FPGA/RTL only.
why: Row hammer flips (fact 9) are strongly data-pattern dependent; enforcing the benign relation claims ~2-5x higher effective threshold.

title: Borrow LCD laser line repair to fix shorts and opens on panels
idea: Apply the display industry's routine laser repair to memory panels, guided by the test map: laser-cut shorts and CVD-write metal across opens on bitlines and wordlines that would otherwise use up redundancy.
why: Yield and fact 7: panel memory yield rises toward ~99% without large spare arrays, cutting periphery and redundancy area.

title: Periodic in-situ microheater anneal heals VRT traps
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: TiN heater strips beside each mat run a few-millisecond 300-400 C local anneal during maintenance windows, with data evacuated to neighbor mats, detrapping the oxide/interface defects behind variable retention time and hammer susceptibility.
why: Resets aging and VRT tails in the field, potentially restoring 2-5x retention in degraded mats and letting cells ship with less end-of-life guardband.

title: Z-channel asymmetric codes matched to true-cell and anti-cell leakage
idea: Optical on-off links lose photons but never create them (the Z-channel). DRAM retention errors are one-way per cell type: true cells go 1->0, anti-cells 0->1. A quick test maps each part's true/anti layout. The FPGA controller then uses asymmetric-error-correcting codes (Varshamov/constant-weight style) that correct t one-way errors with about half the parity symmetric BCH needs.
why: The same parity budget corrects ~2x the retention errors, so refresh intervals can stretch 2-4x (fact 3). It is pure coding plus firmware, which fits the budget.

title: One codeword from CPU core to capacitor: fused link-storage ECC
idea: Combine link CRC/retry with on-die and rank ECC into one end-to-end Reed-Solomon codeword generated in the CPU, carried unchanged over the bus and stored as-is; the DRAM die drops its own ECC engine and the module drops separate ECC chips, while the host decoder corrects both channel and cell errors.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and cost: removes duplicated on-die ECC logic and parity (~6% of die) plus x4 ECC devices while giving weaker cells stronger protection.

title: Substitute fixed VDD/2 bitline precharge with time-since-refresh adaptive reference
idea: Lower the bitline precharge/reference voltage step by step as time since a row's last refresh grows, tracking the drooping stored '1' level, so the sense margin stays balanced as charge leaks.
why: Retention (fact 3): balancing margin late in the interval can give ~1.5-2x longer retention with no cell change.

title: Bit-plane transposition gives each bit significance its own refresh
idea: Po: low bits don't deserve to be remembered. The controller transposes bf16/fp8 tensors into bit planes in separate rows; sign/exponent planes refresh at 64 ms, upper mantissa at 256 ms, and the bottom three mantissa planes at 2 s or never (they are regenerated by the next training step).
why: Refresh (fact 3) for AI tensor regions: ~50-60% fewer refreshes; weak-tail rows can be assigned to LSB planes instead of being repaired.

title: Per-boot keyed Feistel scramble of physical row adjacency
idea: TRIZ #9 Prior counteraction: an on-die 4-round Feistel network keyed by a per-boot random seed permutes logical-to-physical rows within each subarray and is re-keyed incrementally each refresh window, so an attacker cannot know which logical rows sandwich a victim.
why: Double- and many-sided hammer patterns become blind guesses; attack cost rises by about the subarray size (~512x), relaxing the hammer threshold needed for cheaper, denser cells.

title: Substitute DIMM-level ECC with algorithm-based fault tolerance in GEMMs
idea: Store AI weights in ECC-less cheap memory and append row/column checksums to each matrix; matmul kernels verify checksums on the fly and correct single errors or reload the tile on mismatch.
why: Removes 12.5% ECC bit overhead and lets inference run on high-BER bins, raising usable supply ~10-15%.

title: Charge-trap odometer counts each row's activations
idea: Inverts 'activation counting is digital bookkeeping': the single added mask places a trap-rich dielectric under a tiny gate at each wordline end so every activation injects a small charge; during refresh the odometer's threshold shift is sensed to flag hammered rows, then erased.
why: Exact per-row hammer tracking (fact 9) with no SRAM tables or controller involvement, ~0.3% area.

title: Minify hammer-counter updates with 4-bit probabilistic Morris counters
idea: Keep a 4-bit Morris-style approximate counter per row in spare cells. On each activation an on-die LFSR increments it only with probability base^-c, so 4 bits span ~1k-30k activations and the counter is rewritten on only a few percent of activations. Victim refresh fires at a threshold set with a safety margin.
why: Fact 9: per-row activation tracking (PRAC-style) with 4x fewer counter bits and ~10-50x fewer read-modify-write updates, shrinking the tRC penalty of hammer defense.

title: Particle-strike detector strip triggers targeted neighborhood scrubs
idea: Po: memory that feels the bullet. A strip of deliberately charge-sensitive detector cells per bank records the time and position of alpha/neutron strikes; the controller at once scrubs only the rows in that strike's footprint, catching multi-bit clusters before a second hit makes them uncorrectable.
why: Soft errors: permits lighter per-line ECC because clustered multi-bit upsets are handled by locality, and cuts patrol-scrub bandwidth ~10x.

title: Vertical parity row rebuilds any dead row per subarray
idea: Rearrange ECC from horizontal to vertical: each subarray keeps one parity row equal to the XOR of its ~512 rows, with write deltas accumulated in an SRAM buffer and flushed during refresh, so a broken wordline, hammered row or stuck row is rebuilt as an erasure.
why: Turns whole-row failures into correctable erasures for ~0.2% overhead, allowing cheaper, less perfect wordline processing.

title: Kintsugi spares: repair rows built stronger, doubling as high-retention zone
idea: As gold-filled cracks become the strongest part, spare rows are built at relaxed pitch with ~1.5x Cs; repaired rows become the sturdiest, and unused spares are exposed as a long-retention region for page tables and ECC metadata refreshed 8x less often.
why: Turns the ~2-5% spare area from dead silicon into useful, ultra-reliable capacity and protects critical metadata.

title: Deliberate BTI stress re-trims outlier read transistors in field
idea: Bias-temperature instability shifts Vt predictably (dVt ~ t^n, partly permanent). When scrub logs show the same gain cell repeatedly misreading because of a low-Vt read transistor, the controller selects only that cell with a wordline+bitline bias and applies millisecond gate stress, which pushes its Vt back toward the population mean.
why: Self-healing: hard errors are repaired in place with no spares, which keeps capacitorless arrays at full capacity as they age.

title: U.S. memory remanufacturing depots instead of new fabs
idea: Rule: failed memory must be repaired, not replaced. Regional U.S. depots equipped with testers, PPR programmers, die-rework and reball lines receive failed modules from hyperscalers. Most failures are a single die or row, so modules are repaired and returned within days.
why: Raises U.S. manufacturability and value-add without a $15B fab. Each repaired module is supply that does not need a new wafer.

title: Fe: iron-boron pair photodissociation screen bins wafers for retention
idea: A benchtop laser plus photoconductance tool measures minority-carrier lifetime before and after a flash that splits Fe-B pairs, giving interstitial iron per wafer; a 10-person company sells it as incoming-wafer screening that routes iron-rich wafers away from retention-critical products.
why: Iron is a top retention-tail culprit (fact 3); early binning lifts yield and lets fabs qualify wafers grown in non-Spruce-Pine crucibles safely.

title: Magnify heat briefly: in-field bank anneal heals leaky cells
idea: Put thin-film heaters under each bank. In a scheduled maintenance window the controller migrates the bank's data over CXL, heats the bank to ~200C for minutes to anneal hot-carrier/BTI damage and re-passivate interface traps behind leaky and VRT cells, then re-profiles it.
why: Fact 3 plus self-healing: reverses aging so the retention tail stays tight over the part's life; weaker day-one bins become acceptable and service life extends.

title: On-die microheater anneals re-passivate leakage traps in the field
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: standard | integration: monolithic with polysilicon heater meander under each bank | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Every few months the controller migrates one bank's data to a neighbour, heats the bank to ~250 C for ~100 ms, and lets hydrogen re-passivate the interface traps that create GIDL and variable-retention tails.
why: Fact 3: restores aged retention tails and slows refresh-rate growth over device life; ~2x tail improvement claimed.

title: On-die micro-heaters anneal leaky access transistors overnight
idea: Po: chips that heal while they sleep. A polysilicon heater grid under each mat pulses the local array to ~250-300 C for milliseconds during maintenance windows (data migrated out first), annealing interface and gate-oxide traps behind variable-retention-time and GIDL tail cells; the mat is re-profiled and returned to service.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and in-field aging: shrinks the VRT tail that forces worst-case refresh; claimed ~2x retention-tail improvement and recovery of degraded dies in the field.

title: Oxygen-implanted buried-oxide pockets stop storage-node junction leakage
idea: Worse: sit the storage-node junction on bulk silicon, where defects and depletion volume generate leakage current. Flip: implant oxygen locally under each storage-node contact (SIMOX-like, Si and O only) and anneal it into thin buried-oxide pockets that shrink junction area and remove the bulk generation path.
why: Fact 3: cuts the junction-leakage tail several-fold, extending retention 2-4x with no scarce materials.

title: Psychoacoustic masking applied to bit-plane refresh of AI tensors
idea: Adapted from MP3/AAC perceptual coding, which spends bits only where the ear notices: the controller stores bf16/fp8 weights bit-plane transposed so sign, exponent and high-mantissa planes sit in normally refreshed rows while low-mantissa planes sit in rows refreshed 8-16x less often; a per-layer sensitivity score (Hessian trace computed at load) sets how many planes each tensor sends to the slow-refresh zone.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): 40-60% of weight bits tolerate BER ~1e-4 with <0.1% accuracy loss, roughly halving refresh power for weight memory and letting those planes live in weaker, cheaper cells.

title: Fe: let the mantissa rust while exponent bits stay protected
idea: Like a thick iron beam that tolerates surface rust, a model-loading library splits bf16/fp8 weights so sign and exponent bits live in ECC-protected, normally refreshed rows while low mantissa bits sit in rows with 4x relaxed refresh and no ECC.
why: Neural nets tolerate mantissa flips, so ~60% of weight bits get cheaper storage and refresh, letting weaker cells serve inference.

title: Golden-copy flash backing replaces ECC and refresh for weights
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: low-swing | integration: DRAM + NAND in one package | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. Immutable inference weights live in a 0.4 V, ECC-less, refresh-relaxed DRAM region with a 16-bit CRC per 256 B; a CRC failure refetches that line from the packaged NAND golden copy and rewrites it.
why: Constraint: ~6x lower CV^2 plus near-zero refresh gives ~10x amortized energy per access; reliability comes from the backing store, not margin.

title: Three-head tape deck read-after-write verifies dry-cleaned contact writes
idea: Three-head tape decks read each bit back milliseconds after recording to confirm it. Write drivers add a fast verify: right after a write to a row flagged high-resistance, the sense amp re-senses the restored cells before precharge and extends tWR or rewrites only if the level is short, covering contacts that are 2-3x more resistive.
why: Water: lets the fab drop wet HF/SC1 pre-metal and contact cleans for dry remote-plasma cleans, which leave higher contact resistance and slow writes (the tWR failure mode); with dry cleans elsewhere this enables the ~10x ultrapure-water cut, adding tWR only on flagged rows.

title: Pyroelectric film senses heating transients and gates refresh rate
idea: Effect: pyroelectricity. A Sc-doped AlN patch per bank (CMOS-compatible and pyroelectric) outputs current proportional to dT/dt, giving a zero-bias, microsecond heating-event detector; refresh steps up only during and after thermal ramps (for example a GPU power spike), and banks sit at the slow rate while temperature is steady and cool.
why: Refresh is 16-33% of idle power (fact 3): today's slow polled thermal sensors force ~10 C guard bands and a blanket 2x refresh above 85 C; transient-aware refresh removes the guard band, giving ~2x longer average refresh intervals.

title: Delete repair: no spare rows, fuses, or laser repair
idea: Po: the chip arrives broken and that's fine. Redundant rows and columns, fuse banks, and the laser-repair and re-test steps are removed; every manufacturing defect up to 1% of cells is handled by the code as an erasure or error.
why: Periphery and test capital (facts 4, 7): ~3-5% die area and ~10-15% of test/repair cycle time removed.

title: Area-selective molecular monolayer passivates gate-edge GIDL sites
idea: No EUV: on DUV-defined buried-wordline recesses, a self-assembled monolayer deposited only on exposed Si/oxide edges (area-selective ALD inhibitor chemistry) passivates the gate-edge trap sites that cause the GIDL leakage tail. Molecular-scale chemistry stands in for nanometer patterning.
why: Could pull the ≤13 fA tail down ~3-10x so larger, cheaper DUV cells meet longer retention and refresh less.

title: Asymmetric Z-channel codes for one-way charge-loss errors
idea: Flip the symmetric-error assumption: retention and hammer errors in true-cells are almost all 1->0, so the array is built with true-cells only (no anti-cells) so every cell leaks toward the same logical value, and SECDED is replaced by unidirectional-error codes (Bose-Lin / Z-channel LDPC) that need fewer check bits per corrected error.
why: Retention tail + row hammer: ~2x correction strength per parity bit vs symmetric codes, letting refresh interval stretch ~2x at equal reliability.

title: S: vulcanized cross-channel parity rebuilds rows lost to hammer
idea: Like sulfur cross-linking rubber chains, a CXL/FPGA controller keeps the XOR of row N across four channels in a fifth channel, updated on writeback, so a row that on-die ECC reports uncorrectable is rebuilt from the cross-link.
why: Chipkill cannot fix whole-row or multi-chip loss; ~25% capacity overhead buys tolerance of hammer wipeouts and dead dies, enabling cheaper DIMMs.

title: Lizard tail autotomy: self-clearing electrodes isolate capacitor breakdown spots
idea: A lizard sheds its tail to survive: borrowing metallized-film-capacitor self-healing, the top electrode includes a 2-3 nm resistive, easily oxidized layer that clears locally around a breakdown filament, so the cell loses a sliver of area instead of shorting to the plate.
why: TDDB at 125 C for 10 years caps storage-dielectric field; benign breakdowns allow ~20% higher field (more charge or thinner dielectric).

title: Eliminate final test: probe each memory tier before depositing the next
idea: In monolithic <=400 C stacking, add an in-line electrical test after each tier, using temporary probe pads on the top surface. Failing regions are logged into a defect map in the base logic die before the next tier buries them.
why: Catches defects while routing around them is still cheap, and turns per-tier yield learning from months into days, speeding the stacked-memory ramp (fact 2).

title: Test-reject DRAM dies sold as graded AI cache memory
idea: Reverse the reject bin into a product line: dies failing retention or hammer specs are packaged into 'Grade-R' modules with published per-row maps, sold for KV caches and recomputable buffers with host software ECC and short-TTL use at ~40% of prime price.
why: Raises usable bit supply by recovering several % of wafer output now scrapped or down-binned, with zero new fab capex.

title: Al: self-passivating pages escalate ECC in place like alumina
idea: Like aluminum growing oxide only where exposed, controller RTL escalates a page to a stronger mode (extra symbols borrowed from a metadata carve-out, or duplicate plus checksum) the moment it logs a correctable error, leaving the rest of memory at lean ECC.
why: Spends ECC overhead only on weak cells, keeping average overhead ~12.5% while approaching strong-ECC reliability, which makes weaker DIMMs acceptable.

title: Bicycle chain: spatially coupled LDPC links codewords along a row
idea: Each 64 B line's parity also covers slices of its neighbors like chain links, forming a spatially coupled LDPC across a 1 KB page that a sliding-window decoder in the base/buffer die resolves while the page is open.
why: Near-capacity correction at ~6% overhead versus 12.5%, tolerating raw BER ~1e-4: enough to use much smaller Cs or far longer refresh.

title: Eliminate per-tier perfection: vertical RAID parity tier in monolithic stacks
idea: In a monolithic stack of N memory tiers built at <=400 C, one tier in every 8 holds XOR parity for the vertical column of cells. A tier region lost to a deposition defect, crack or later failure is rebuilt from the other tiers on read, so stack yield no longer falls as Y^N.
why: Breaks the compound-yield barrier that makes 26+ tier stacks uneconomic (fact 2); 12.5% overhead buys tolerance of whole-tier defect regions.

title: Overclocker binning in reverse: weak-retention dies sold as refresh-class parts
idea: Overclockers profile each module's true margins and tune timings to match. Do the reverse for retention: dies that fail 64 ms but pass 32 ms get a 'refresh class' written into vendor bytes of the standard SPD, and the BIOS sets the controller's existing programmable tREFI or 2x-refresh mode to suit.
why: Retention-fail dies are scrapped or burn spare rows today. Selling them as 2x-refresh parts for lightly loaded or cool servers recovers several percent of wafer output (fact 3).

title: Minify each 3D cell, magnify copies: three-tier majority bits
idea: Lateral 3D DRAM cells only fit ~1 fF capacitors. Instead of chasing bigger ones, write each bit to the same x-y position on three tiers through a shared vertical bitline and resolve it with a 3-input majority sense amp. Tiers are cheap deposition steps; capacitor aspect ratio is not.
why: Fact 2: removes the capacitor blocker for 3D. Per-cell BER 1e-3 becomes ~3e-6 after voting (3p^2), and 3x tiers of 1 fF cells beats waiting for a 5 fF lateral capacitor.

title: Apoptotic cascade: retire a failing page's predicted spatial accomplices
idea: Apoptotic cells signal their neighbours; when the OS retires a page for a hard error, a learned fault-cluster model of the die (shared wordline, bitline, sub-wordline driver, TSV column) pre-emptively migrates and retires the physically co-located pages most likely to fail next, before they produce uncorrectable errors.
why: Field reliability of weaker, cheaper bins: most uncorrectable errors come from spatially clustered faults; pre-emptive retirement could cut UE rates ~5-10x for <0.1% capacity, letting marginal dies ship.

title: C: graphene-hex interleave spreads clustered flips across codewords
idea: Map codeword bits onto physical columns and chips in a honeycomb pattern, so bits that are physical neighbors (which fail together from shared defects or hammer hot zones) always fall in different codewords, each seeing at most one bad symbol. A remap table in controller RTL.
why: Turns clustered multi-bit failures (facts 8-9) into single-symbol errors that existing SEC or chipkill corrects; claim ~10x fewer uncorrectable events.

title: Twin landing-pad contacts survive stochastic misses from PFAS-free resists
idea: Rearrange each storage-node contact from one landing pad into two half-size pads in parallel: tin-oxo metal-oxide EUV resists without fluorinated photo-acid generators print more stochastic missing contacts, but a cell now fails only if both pads miss, squaring the defect rate.
why: Contact stochastic failure falls from ~1e-7 to ~1e-14 per cell, allowing PFAS-free resists without yield loss for a few % area.

title: Hydrocarbon-refrigerant chilled memory tier that barely refreshes
idea: Flip from refreshing hot memory to chilling it: a capacity-tier DRAM shelf is held near -20 C by propane (R290) or CO2 (R744) vapor-compression loops instead of HFC refrigerants or fluorinated immersion fluids, stretching retention ~1000x so refresh drops to seconds.
why: Refresh power and bandwidth nearly removed and cells with ~10x lower Cs become usable; chiller power offsets part of the gain.

title: Magnify row pitch on cheap glass area to starve row hammer
idea: Processed glass area costs ~500-1000x less per cm^2 than DRAM-fab silicon, so space wordlines 3x farther apart with grounded shield lines between them. The insulating substrate also removes the shared bulk path for injected charge.
why: Fact 9: coupling falls steeply with pitch, so the hammer threshold could rise from ~1k to >100k activations, removing mitigation logic and its tRC tax.

title: Weak cells hold only clean pages, re-fetched on error
idea: Rearrange placement by dirtiness: pages with an intact copy in flash or CXL far memory (weights, code, read-mostly caches) go to cheap weak-retention DRAM protected only by a 16-bit CRC, and a CRC failure triggers a re-fetch instead of correction; a line is migrated to strong ECC banks on its first write.
why: Lets ~60-80% of inference-server capacity use reject-grade or long-refresh cells; ECC overhead on that share drops from 12.5% to ~3%.

title: Al-strapped TiN wordlines with per-row variable latency
idea: Worse: keep tungsten (China ~80%) buried wordlines because cheaper conductors are too resistive. Flip: build buried wordlines from TiN plus heavily doped Si, strapped every 256 cells with Al lines, and let the controller use per-row measured tRCD/tRAS so the few slow far-end rows get extra cycles instead of forcing global worst-case timing.
why: Scarce resources and U.S. manufacturability: removes W from the array while keeping average latency within ~5% via variable-latency timing.

title: Eliminate the storage-node junction: junctionless accumulation-mode access transistors
idea: Replace the n+/p junction at the storage node with a uniformly doped junctionless (accumulation-mode) channel. This removes the high-field depletion region where trap-assisted tunneling and GIDL create the leakage tail.
why: Attacks the <=13 fA tail (fact 3); if the tail tightens 10x, refresh intervals stretch ~10x, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss.

title: PFAS-free certified DRAM grade paired with system-level ECC
idea: Flip the constraint into a market: define a certified PFAS-free DRAM grade for public buyers and hyperscaler sustainability targets, specified at relaxed raw BER and retention and sold with mandatory system-level ECC and per-row refresh, so new fabs without fluorinated steps can sell from day one.
why: Raises supply from simpler new fabs, pre-empts the proposed EU universal PFAS restriction and strengthens US manufacturability.

title: Solar bypass diodes: segment switches replace column redundancy
idea: Adapted from photovoltaic panels, whose bypass diodes route current around a shaded or failed string instead of losing the panel: each bitline is split into 4 segments joined by small pass switches; a segment with a defect (short, leaky cluster) is opened and its cells skipped via a decoder offset, so only a quarter-column is lost instead of swapping in a full redundant column.
why: Periphery and repair area (fact 7): spare columns plus fuses and muxes cost several percent of area; segment bypass trades ~1-2% switch overhead for removing most column redundancy and lets arrays ship with more local defects.

title: Rounded trench and junction corners to clip GIDL tail
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality/curvature: a hydrogen anneal reflows silicon so buried-wordline trench bottoms and storage-node contact edges reach radii of 3 nm or more, lowering the peak junction field that drives trap-assisted tunnelling in the worst cells.
why: Fact 3: 20-30% lower peak field can cut tail leakage ~5-10x (exponential in field), stretching refresh ~4x.

title: Bit-significance tiering: mantissa LSBs live in unrefreshed soft rows
idea: Ideal: errors that cost nothing because they do not matter. Closest: the memory controller splits each bf16/fp8 tensor word, storing sign, exponent and top mantissa bits in refreshed ECC rows and the low mantissa bits in 'soft rows' with 1 s refresh and no ECC, where rare decays add noise below quantization noise.
why: Facts 3 and 1: ~40% of AI tensor bits need no fast refresh or ECC; refresh power ~-35%, ECC overhead removed on that fraction, and soft rows can use smaller Cs.

title: Weaver's warp and weft: codewords across nozzles, never along web
idea: A weaver knows faults run along the warp: inkjet nozzle failures and roller scratches leave long streaks in the machine direction, so the address mapping spreads each ECC codeword's bits across different nozzle tracks in the cross-web direction, and a dead nozzle costs at most one bit per codeword.
why: Correlated streak defects that would overwhelm ECC become independent single-bit errors that SECDED or BCH handles; required ECC strength for printed memory could fall ~2-4x.

title: Ce: ceria oxygen-storage interlayer self-heals capacitor dielectric vacancies
idea: Insert ~1 nm CeO2 between the TiN electrode and ZrO2 dielectric; ceria cycles Ce3+/Ce4+ as in automotive catalytic converters, absorbing oxygen vacancies and releasing oxygen to buffer the vacancy profile that drives leakage drift and breakdown.
why: Lets capacitors run thinner, higher-capacitance dielectrics (fact 1) without lifetime leakage creep; target ~2x higher allowed field.

title: Jazz wrong notes: bit-plane retention tiers for AI weights and KV-cache
idea: In jazz a wrong note resolves into the next; BF16/FP8 tensors are stored transposed by bit-plane, with sign/exponent/high-mantissa planes in normally refreshed rows and low-mantissa planes in rows with 8-16x longer refresh and no ECC, where flips dissolve into model noise.
why: Fact 3: roughly half of AI bits tolerate 1e-4 BER, cutting refresh power and ECC overhead on half the capacity.

title: Navigator's chart: printed thermistor skin sets refresh per die
idea: A navigator wants a detailed local chart, not one compass: an array of NTC thermistor-ink pads and silver traces is screen-printed onto the DIMM PCB or interposer next to every DRAM die or bank region and read by the module PMIC, so the controller sets each die's refresh interval from its local temperature rather than from the hottest sensor.
why: Fact 3: dies in real racks differ by 10-20 C, so per-die refresh saves an estimated 15-30% of refresh energy for pennies of ink.

title: Substitute hydrogen passivation with deuterium anneal of access transistors
idea: Replace the forming-gas H2 anneal of the array with a high-pressure D2 anneal; Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier and field-driven depassivation, so fewer interface traps are generated over life.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and hammer trap generation (fact 9): fewer trap-assisted leakage outliers can tighten the retention tail and slow wear-out of hammer margin; a low-capex process swap.

title: Activation-rate billing makes row hammer an economic problem
idea: Po: hammering is legal but expensive. Cloud hypervisors meter each VM's per-row activation density from memory-controller counters, bill activation bursts beyond a budget, and throttle or live-migrate tenants whose activation pattern looks adversarial.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) in shared clouds: lowers reliance on costly in-DRAM mitigation, letting cheaper low-threshold dies be deployed safely.

title: 64-activation cap: hot rows migrate into on-die SRAM
idea: Imposed limit: no row may be activated more than 64 times per refresh window. When a row hits the cap, its contents are copied into a small on-die hot-row SRAM (or a latched spare sense-amp stripe) and served from there for the rest of the window. The DRAM row is never re-opened.
why: Fact 9: row hammer becomes impossible at any threshold above 64, independent of cell weakness, and hot rows also get faster access.

title: Tungsten-free buried wordlines tolerate a slow far-end tail
idea: Po: wordlines with no tungsten. Buried wordlines use a TiN liner with heavily doped polysilicon fill instead of W; the higher RC under-drives far-end cells within the tRCD window, producing a ~1% incomplete-restore tail at mat edges that the code corrects.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%): removes the largest W use in the DRAM front end with no density loss.

title: Eliminate refresh for compiler-proven short-lived tensor pages
idea: Stop treating refresh as a service every page gets. The ML compiler/runtime proves that each activation or KV buffer is rewritten or freed within T_live (typically under 5 ms) and tags its pages with a page-table 'lifetime' bit. The controller's refresh engine then skips any row whose last write is younger than the measured worst-case retention minus a margin.
why: Refresh (~46 fJ/bit, 10-20% bandwidth, fact 3): 60-80% of AI DRAM traffic is short-lived, so refresh operations drop ~3-5x, and weaker-retention cells become acceptable for those pages.

title: Substitute one-way STT read currents with disturb-immune state encoding
idea: STT read current can only disturb one state (e.g., P to AP in the read direction); store each word with an inversion flag chosen so most cells sit in the immune state, and keep flags in larger high-barrier MTJs.
why: Read disturb limits MRAM read current and speed; halving at-risk cells lets ~1.5-2x higher read current for DRAM-class latency.

title: FeRAM read fatigue removed by sub-coercive nondestructive capacitance readout
idea: Ramtron-era FeRAM's destructive read made every read a write, fatiguing cells and costing restore energy. Fix: read with a small sub-coercive AC probe that senses the polarization-dependent asymmetry of the capacitor's C-V curve (piezo/dielectric nonlinearity), leaving the domain state untouched.
why: Nonvolatile and refresh-free; reads consume no endurance, so ~1e10-cycle HZO acts as effectively unlimited endurance for read-heavy data, and no restore cycle is needed (fact 8).

title: Lesion-wiring: fine-tune each model on its own DIMM's fault map
idea: Like a developing brain rewiring around a lesion, an accelerator profiles its own HBM's weak-cell map at a relaxed 1 s refresh, then runs a short fine-tune in which exactly those weight bits are clamped to their decayed values, so the deployed model stops depending on them and weight regions run permanently at the relaxed refresh.
why: Refresh bandwidth/energy (10-20% bandwidth at 32-64 Gb) and retention tail: weights are most of inference HBM capacity; ~16x longer refresh there with <0.1% accuracy loss frees bandwidth and idle power.

title: Thick dielectric collar at the capacitor's leaky top rim
idea: Inverts 'capacitor dielectric must be uniform': one mask defines a thicker, lower-k oxide collar at the pillar top, where field crowding at electrode corners concentrates leakage and early breakdown.
why: Capacitor leakage and breakdown tail cut ~2-5x for <5% Cs loss, shrinking the retention tail and allowing a thinner, higher-k main dielectric.

title: Thermoelectric-cooled HBM stacks traded for 4x longer refresh
idea: Combine an in-package Peltier stage between GPU and HBM stack with temperature-indexed refresh: holding the DRAM ~20 C cooler roughly quadruples retention (leakage roughly doubles per ~10 C), so the refresh interval stretches and weak cells pass.
why: Refresh costs 16-33% of idle power and 10-20% of bandwidth (fact 3): recovers most of it in hot AI packages; Peltier power offsets part of the energy, but bandwidth gain is net.

title: Lighthouse rotation: a vacated rotating subarray enables continuous online stress testing
idea: One subarray per bank is always empty and the vacancy sweeps around the bank like a lighthouse beam (data moved by in-DRAM row copy); while empty, it is stress-tested at full speed for retention, hammer and VRT and the weak map is updated with no downtime.
why: Aging and VRT invalidate fab profiles; continuous safe profiling enables aggressive 4x profile-guided refresh and early retirement for ~1.5% capacity.

title: Store the recipe, not the parity: lineage recompute on error
idea: Inverts 'memory must correct its own errors': for recomputable tensors (activations, decompressed weights, caches) the runtime replaces SECDED with a 4-bit detection CRC plus a pointer to the producing kernel; on a detected error it recomputes only the affected tile from its inputs.
why: Halves ECC overhead for recomputable data and tolerates ~100x higher BER, permitting much longer refresh; recompute cost is negligible at realistic error rates.

title: Substitute tungsten spin-orbit layers with titanium or chromium orbital torque
idea: Replace W/Ta/Pt spin-Hall layers in SOT-MRAM with light 3d metals (Ti, Cr) that produce torque through the orbital Hall effect, converted at a Ni interface; the write current never crosses the MgO barrier.
why: Unlimited endurance (no barrier stress), plus removal of tungsten (China ~80%) and platinum dependence; a U.S.-supply-friendly NV cell.

title: Self-clearing film-capacitor electrodes for thin high-k DRAM capacitors
idea: Adapted from metallized polymer film capacitors, whose ultra-thin electrode vaporizes around a breakdown spot so the part survives with negligibly less area: use a 2-3 nm top electrode of a low-melting conductive oxide so a local dielectric breakdown burns a sub-10-nm hole in the electrode, isolating the defect instead of shorting the cell.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): dielectric thickness is set by breakdown and leakage tails; tolerating pinholes could allow ~20-30% thinner high-k and proportionally higher Cs or lower aspect ratio without yield loss to shorted cells.

title: Actuarially insured B-grade DRAM on FPGA-CXL cards
idea: Outlets sell factory 'seconds' with a warranty attached. Buy retention-rejected or down-binned dies and modules (fail at 64 ms, pass at 32 ms; sold 10-30% cheaper or scrapped). Mount them behind an FPGA CXL controller that refreshes at 2x and applies strong symbol ECC, and price the warranty from logged error data. Pilot 1,000 cards within the $1M budget.
why: Turns a scrap stream into usable capacity during the 4x shortage, at an estimated 30-50% lower cost per bit and no new wafer capital (fact 4).

title: Recycling sorter: sell retention-binned 'harvest grade' DRAM with mandated controller ECC
idea: Dies failing JEDEC 64 ms retention but passing at 16 ms or under stronger ECC are graded into a new SKU for AI KV-cache and cold-tier buyers whose controllers run 4x refresh or LDPC, with a standard grade label and warranty model so the parts are bankable.
why: Recovers ~5-15% of wafer output now scrapped or downgraded; pure supply gain without new fabs, helium or EUV.

title: Food freshness label: on-die Arrhenius dose integrator for life-aware derating
idea: Like time-temperature indicator labels on food, a tiny on-die structure (a floating node leaking through thermally activated oxide, cross-checked by a BTI ring oscillator) integrates cumulative thermal stress; firmware reads the 'age' and tightens refresh, VNWL and ECC mode as the dose nears 10 years at 125 C equivalent.
why: Parts in milder missions run ~2x relaxed refresh while hot ones are protected to the 125 C/10-year budget; cuts lifetime guard-band ~20-30%.

title: Venus-lander electronics: SiC access transistors for refresh-free cells
idea: NASA's SiC JFET circuits have run for weeks at 460 C because SiC's intrinsic carrier density is ~10^19 times lower than silicon's. Bond a thin 4H-SiC (or beta-Ga2O3) access-transistor layer onto a silicon periphery wafer, so each cell's off-state leakage is in the attoamps and retention lasts minutes to hours even at 125 C.
why: Attacks the access-transistor leakage tail (fact 3) beyond the IGZO prior work, and holds up at high temperature, where IGZO is weaker. Refresh nearly disappears and Cs could drop ~5x (fact 1).

title: Self-healing microcapsule underfill for hybrid-bonded memory stacks
idea: Self-healing concrete and composites release a healing agent when cracks open; fill HBM/3D-stack gaps with underfill holding microcapsules of low-viscosity resin plus dispersed catalyst that rupture at TSV or micro-bump cracks during thermal cycling and re-bond them, using no rare-gas processing.
why: Reduces TSV/bump field failures and cycling yield loss (fact 6: 20-30% yield hit), allowing thinner, cheaper stacks with less conservative design margins.

title: Domestic molybdenum dual-work-function buried wordline replaces tungsten
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: tungsten (China ~80%) is replaced by molybdenum from U.S. mines in the buried wordline; Mo needs no thick TiN barrier, which frees room for a low-work-function lower segment next to the storage-node junction that softens the gate-to-drain field.
why: Removes the tungsten chokepoint, cuts GIDL in tail cells ~3-5x and lowers wordline resistance ~20-30% in narrow trenches: a refresh and supply-security win.

title: Relaxed DUV array bonded to logic doing per-mat BCH
idea: Box [medium: capacitor at relaxed 18 nm | access: vertical channel | sense: on bonded logic wafer | integration: wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV-only array + advanced logic]. The array wafer skips EUV and accepts ~1e-4 raw BER, while the bonded logic wafer runs a t=8 BCH decoder beside every 512-bit mat word through ~1 um pitch bonds.
why: Facts 4/7: removes 5-7 EUV layers from the array and moves periphery off the array die; ~30% lower cost per bit.

title: FD-SOI back-gate trims each subarray's leakage over its lifetime
idea: No EUV: build the access array on DUV FD-SOI and give each subarray its own back-gate bias rail. Firmware re-trims back-bias yearly as aging shifts thresholds, keeping each subarray's leakage tail centered.
why: Tightens the retention distribution ~3-5x over life, allowing longer refresh on coarse-node silicon.

title: Oxygen-vacancy back gate trims every leaky row after test
idea: Effect: field-driven oxygen-vacancy drift in HfOx. Each stacked thin-film tier has a back-gate dielectric of oxygen-deficient HfOx; after retention test, a forming-like pulse drifts vacancies toward or away from the channel, permanently shifting a tail row's Vt by ~+100 mV: a non-volatile per-row analog leakage fuse.
why: 10x density: cheap thin-film tiers have broad Vt spreads, and per-row trim collapses the tail so low-cost channels meet retention in 32-tier stacks (~10x). Same cost: the back gate is one extra deposition per tier.

title: Organ-donor program: retired DIMMs reborn as a CXL cold tier
idea: Po: dead memory comes back to life. Hyperscalers route decommissioned DDR4/DDR5 through a retest line that builds per-die weak-row maps, then mount the modules behind CXL controllers with strong ECC and map-based row retirement as a cold memory tier for VMs and caches.
why: Supply: reuses millions of DIMMs a year; 10-20% of server capacity demand could be served by second-life parts at <30% of new-part cost during the shortage.

title: Cobalt-free Fe/MgO junctions store a field-updatable repair map
idea: Worse: rely on one-shot laser or e-fuse repair, so cells that weaken after shipment can never be fixed. Flip: put a small array of Fe/MgO/Fe magnetic tunnel junctions (no Co, Ta or Ru) on-die as rewritable repair memory; their lower TMR is acceptable with write-verify and redundancy, and spares can be reassigned in the field indefinitely.
why: Self-healing and yield: in-field repair cuts returns and lets makers ship with tighter spare budgets, avoiding the Co/Ru/Ta that standard MRAM needs.

title: Shared plate line reads a row's popcount as a checksum
idea: Reverse plate and bitline roles for detection: the plate electrode of each row segment (TiN from TiCl4) is sensed during activation, and its displacement charge is proportional to the number of charged cells, giving an analog popcount compared against a stored count to flag flips without per-word parity bits.
why: Error detection for ~0.5% overhead vs 6-12% ECC parity, freeing area for larger-footprint, fluorine-free low-AR capacitors.

title: Idle-time self-hammering maps each row's true flip threshold
idea: Reverse attacker and defender: in idle windows the controller copies a row aside, hammers it with known patterns, records the activation count at first flip, and programs per-row thresholds into mitigation logic, re-running as the chip ages.
why: Row hammer: most rows tolerate far more than the worst-case 1k, so tailored thresholds cut mitigation refreshes ~5-10x.

title: Ship-then-learn: dies finish retention testing inside customer servers
idea: Worse: hold every die in hours-long, worst-case retention testers. Flip: ship after a short screen with conservative 32 ms refresh, then let the module's own BIST profile each row's retention during its first weeks of idle time and gradually relax refresh to measured values, uploading the map to the controller.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): retention test is a large share of test-floor capital and cycle time; moving it into the field could cut test cost 30-50% and shorten time to market.

title: Minify replacement unit: swappable foil-memory cartridges with wear telemetry
idea: Make oxide-TFT memory roll-to-roll on polyimide or steel foil and package it as cheap hot-swap cartridges. Each reports ECC-correction and retention telemetry and is swapped like an ink cartridge when it crosses a threshold, so cells only need a 2-3 year life.
why: Capital and cost: roll-to-roll lines cost a sliver of a fab; the business model takes per-cell lifetime requirements out of the spec.

title: Z-channel codes exploit leakage's one-way arrow of time
idea: Time-direction shift: true-cells only decay 1->0 and anti-cells only 0->1, so the error channel is asymmetric. Encode with asymmetric (Z-channel/Berger-style constant-weight) codes, matched to the true/anti layout, that spend parity only on the one possible flip direction.
why: Corrects about 2x more retention errors per parity bit than symmetric SECDED/BCH, permitting ~30% lower Cs or a longer refresh interval at equal reliability.

title: Row-wide product code computed at activation exploits overfetch
idea: Every ACT already senses a full 8 Kb row (128x overfetch), so all bits sit in the sense amps for free. Place a 2D product code (row checksum plus column parity over 64x128 tiles) in the sense-amp stripe and correct multi-bit clusters before the column read.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) becomes reliability: code rate ~97% vs 94%, and clustered weak-cell failures get corrected.

title: Substitute charge-trap endurance limits with periodic microheater self-annealing
idea: Fast-write charge-trap (SONOS-like) NV cells get buried microheaters per block; when ECC errors climb, a ms-scale ~800 C local anneal empties damaged traps and repairs the tunnel oxide, resetting wear.
why: Endurance: anneal-and-heal can push charge-trap cells from ~1e6 to >1e9+ cycles, closer to working memory; uses mature fab processes, no EUV.

title: Neurobiologist's myelin: grounded shield lines insulate wordlines from hammer
idea: Myelin insulates axons so signals don't leak into neighbors: insert a buried, grounded (or slightly negatively biased) shield conductor between every pair of active buried wordlines to absorb hammer-injected electrons and cut the capacitive and passing-gate coupling.
why: Fact 9: the hammer threshold could rise from ~1k to 50k+ activations at ~10% array area, partly paid back by removing TRR/RFM logic and bandwidth.

title: P: buried phosphorus collector line sweeps hammer-injected electrons away
idea: A deep n+ phosphorus stripe runs between adjacent rows under the passing wordline, biased slightly positive, acting as a drain that collects electrons emitted from traps when aggressor wordlines toggle, before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Device-level row hammer (fact 9) mitigation that needs no counters or extra refresh; claim ~5-10x higher first-flip activation count.

title: Mg2Si thermoelectric spots cool only the weakest mats
idea: Worse: chill the whole module to rescue a few weak, hot mats. Flip: integrate thin-film Mg2Si / higher-manganese-silicide Peltier elements under the mats that test-time profiling marks as retention-weak, driven only when those mats exceed a temperature, so the weak tail sees ~10 C cooler silicon.
why: Fact 3 and yield: rescues retention-weak dies and mats with only Mg, Si and Mn.

title: Tuned-mass-damper resonance detector: spectral hammer detection without counters
idea: A tuned mass damper targets one resonant frequency of a building. Hammering is periodic, so each bank runs a few Goertzel/autocorrelation bins over a hashed row-address stream. Aggressor sequences that recur at a fixed lag, including many-sided TRRespass patterns, stand out using about 10-20 registers. The detected aggressors get neighbour refresh.
why: Tracking SRAM could shrink ~90% compared with per-row counters (PRAC) while catching patterns that sampling TRR misses (facts 7 and 9).

title: Word-granular remap CAM absorbs directed-self-assembly line defects
idea: No EUV: pattern ~12 nm pitch wordlines with block-copolymer directed self-assembly on DUV guide patterns, accepting the ~0.1-1/cm2 dislocation defects. Scale shift (molecular dislocation -> 64-bit word): each defect is mapped at sort and absorbed by a per-bank content-addressable remap of 64-bit words.
why: Reaches near-EUV pitch without EUV tools (saves ~5-7 EUV layers of capex), with defect tolerance at a ~0.5% periphery cost.

title: Cut the cell plate into strips and bump it on reads
idea: Inverts 'the cell plate is a passive common electrode': one mask cuts the plate into row-group strips; when a row with known weak cells is read, its strip is pulsed +0.2-0.3 V just before sensing so capacitive coupling lifts the storage node and the bitline signal.
why: ~30% more sense signal for weak cells (facts 1, 3), so smaller Cs or longer refresh becomes tolerable; one non-critical mask.

title: Pothole map: temperature-binned weak maps convert errors into erasures
idea: Like a road crew's pothole map, the controller keeps compact weak-cell maps per temperature bin (85/105/125 C) learned in-field; at the current temperature those positions are decoded as erasures, which cost half as much as unknown errors in RS/BCH.
why: At 125 C the weak set is large but predictable; roughly doubles effective ECC strength and allows 2-4x longer hot refresh across the 10-year life.

title: Dithered multi-comparator sensing reads four-level cells reliably
idea: Effect: stochastic resonance and dithering. After charge sharing the bitline voltage holds for a few ns; three coarse comparators shared per 8 bitlines sample it several times with injected calibrated dither, and averaging resolves below comparator offset, reading 4 levels (2 bits) from a ~0.8 fF cell before a DAC-driven restore.
why: 10x density: 2 bits/cell times a 12-tier stack of ~0.8 fF cells (~5x) gives ~10x bits/mm^2. Same cost: comparators and DACs are amortized across 8 bitlines, with no capacitor module.
